newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Mourning for haj fire victims marks Moslem holiday.
newsitem.headline: Mourning for haj fire victims marks Moslem holiday.

text.p: World Moslems prepared for the Eid al-Adha feast on Thursday at the end of the haj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia, but the usually joyous day was marked by mourning for 343 pilgrims who died in a fire that swept through their tent camp.
The blaze also injured 1,290 people when it gutted 70,000 tents on Tuesday on the plain of Mena, about 11 km (seven miles) from the Islamic holy city of Mecca.
While officials struggle to identify the dead, treat the injured and shelter people stranded by the blaze, the two million pilgrims in the kingdom will perform the final rituals of haj.
At dawn, crowds of pilgrims in seamless white robes will hurl stones at pillars symbolising the devil on the outskirts of Mecca, site of a stampede which killed 270 people in 1994.

They will shave their heads, and to mark the end of the pilgrimage they will slaughter hundreds of thousands of sheep and cattle for Eid al-Adha (the Feast of Sacrifice), which is also celebrated by some one billion Moslems around the world.
But not everyone will be able to join in the festivities.

Saudi television showed many of the fire's victims in hospital beds, some of them old and frail, others young and afraid. One bandaged child stared into the camera with a face distorted with pain. Many patients displayed badly burns.

Victims of the fire -- many of them in critical condition -- had been rushed to 12 nearby hospitals, and specialised medical centres several hours away were on high alert in case seriously injured victims had to be transferred.
The official media did not give the nationalities of the dead but diplomats said most of them were Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis.
Saudi newspapers said the fire also engulfed Syrian, Lebanese, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni and Moroccan sections of the camp.
Diplomats said identification was difficult as many bodies were charred beyond recognition.

"Investigations indicate that the fire was an accident," Saudi Arabia's ambassador in London Ghazi Algosaibi said in a statement. "We are faced with a human tragedy which has no political implications."
Diplomats and witnesses said the blaze was caused by gas cylinder explosions but Riyadh gave no cause.
Diplomats said earlier they feared the death toll might rise from the fire, which had spread panic among thousands of pilgrims performing one of Islam's holiest rites.

In Mena on Wednesday, the air was still thick with the smell of smoke and the ground was littered with debris, such as burnt-out buses and charred water bottles. Trucks carted off blackened rubble, while workers -- helped by the Saudi army -- hurried to erect new tents.
Undeterred by the tragedy, the pilgrims continued with the haj rituals and scrambled up Mount Arafat where the Prophet Mohammed gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago.
Moslems traditionally sleep at the encampment in Mena before their trek to Mount Arafat, the pinnacle of an elaborate set of haj rituals. The prayers at Arafat mark the climax of haj.
Pilgrims marched to Arafat with prayer rugs slung over their shoulders, carrying plastic water bottles and umbrellas to cope with the 40 Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) heat.
On their way, many chanted "I have answered your call, God, there is no God but you". A blind cleric gave the traditional midday sermon at Arafat, but made no reference to the disaster.

Ambassador Algosaibi said: "The fire at Mena and the ensuing loss of life and the injuries is a tragedy for all Moslems. The custodian of the Two Holy Mosques, King Fahd bin Abdul-Aziz, expressed his sympathy and condolences to the families of the victims. It is a sentiment the whole Saudi people shares."

The blaze was the latest tragedy to strike the pilgrimage to Mecca. Able-bodied Moslems are obliged to make haj at least once if they can afford it. In 1990, 1,426 pilgrims were crushed to death in a stampede in a tunnel. In 1995, three people were killed when a fire swept through the tent camps at Mena after Saudi Arabians lit a stove in their tent.
